claims.text: The as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a mixed microstructure dominated by metastable solid solutions with a limited fraction of intermetallic phases.
Thermal ageing drives a diffusion-mediated transformation from metastable solid solutions toward a more stable intermetallic-containing mixture.
Precipitation of intermetallic phases during ageing causes local elemental redistribution that changes the surface composition.
Ageing enhances segregation of elements such as Mg, Ti, Zn, or Cu at the alloy surface.
Surface elemental redistribution facilitates formation of a more uniform, continuous, and adherent passivating oxide film.
A protective passivating surface film mitigates corrosive attack and increases corrosion resistance.
The passivating oxide film improves high-temperature oxidation performance.
The as-processed baseline has limited passivating oxide-film formation.
Thermally aged samples will contain a higher fraction of stable intermetallic phases than as-processed samples.
Thermally aged samples will develop more uniform and adherent surface oxide films than as-processed samples.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit lower corrosion current densities than as-processed samples.
Thermally aged samples will show reduced oxidation mass gain or reduced scale spallation relative to as-processed samples.
The proposed mechanism applies to alloys whose overall density remains below 6 g/cm3.
The mechanism requires ageing sufficient for diffusion-controlled transformation but insufficient to cause full homogenization or loss of alloy integrity.
Controlled thermal-processing history can change phase morphology in a non-equilibrium high-entropy alloy without eliminating compositional partitioning.
In Mg-Ti-Zn alloys, Ti and Zn in the matrix together with fine intermetallics promote a protective surface film and low corrosion current density.
